etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English performen, parfournen (“to perform”), from Anglo-Norman performer, parfourmer, alteration of Old French parfornir, parfurnir (“to complete, accomplish, perform”), from par- + fornir, furnir (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Frankish *frummjan (“to accomplish, furnish”), from Proto-Germanic *frumjaną, *framjaną (“to further, promote”), from Proto-Indo-European *promo- (“in front, forth”), *per- (“forward, out”). Cognate with Old High German frummen (“to do, execute, accomplish, provide”), Old Saxon frummian (“to perform, promote”), Old English fremman (“to perform, execute, carry out, accomplish”), Gothic 𐍆𐍂𐌿𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (frumjan, “to promote, accomplish”). See also frame, from. Modernly, rather than Proto-Germanic *frumjaną, associated with Latin formō, analyzable as per- + form.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Lee S. Langston, “The Adaptable Gas Turbine”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Turbines have been around for a long time—windmills and water wheels are early examples. The name comes from the Latin turbo, meaning vortex, and thus the defining property of a turbine is that a fluid or gas turns the blades of a rotor, which is attached to a shaft that can perform useful work.

definitions.definition: (sexology, uncommon) Of a man, to be able to initiate or fulfill an act of sexual intercourse.
(intransitive) To exhibit an expected pattern of behavior; to function; to work.

quote.citation: 2003, “P.I.M.P.”, in Get Rich or Die Tryin', performed by 50 Cent:
quote.text: I could care less how she perform when she in the bed

definitions.definition: (transitive) To act in accordance with (a contract); to fulfill one’s terms of (a contract).
(law) To act in a way set forth in a contract.
(transitive, intransitive) To do (something) in front of an audience, such as acting or music, often in order to entertain.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Perform a part thou hast not done before.

definitions.definition: (by extension, transitive) To behave theatrically so as to give the impression of (a quality, character trait, etc.); to feign.

quote.citation: 2021, David Edgerton, “The one good thing to come out of Brexit: a bonfire of national illusions”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: As things now stand, Brexit is a pointless gesture, a politics of headlines in which sovereignty is performed by bleating world-beating absurdities.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To behave in accordance with, and thereby in turn shape, (a social notion or role).

quote.citation: 2022 September 9, Sophie Gilbert, “No One Performed Britishness Better Than Her Majesty”, in The Atlantic‎[2]:
quote.text: Even before her seven decades as monarch began, she performed Britishness more intuitively than anyone ever had, or likely ever will again.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To behave in ways that carry meaning in social contexts.
(social sciences) Of a social actor, to behave in certain ways.
